PART A — SYSTEMS DESIGN DOCUMENT
A0. Reference systems and what we take from each

Three classes of prior art inform this design. None is forkable as-is: the SaaS-hosted memory platforms ship client code publicly while the engine stays proprietary, and the pure-OSS enterprise search tools lack a memory layer and video pipeline.

Enterprise search / connector breadth — Onyx (formerly Danswer). The most instructive self-hostable analog: MIT core with an Enterprise license for ee/, 40+ connectors, permission-aware retrieval that mirrors source ACLs, hybrid search + reranking + a knowledge graph, background sync workers (Redis + MinIO), SSO (OIDC/SAML), and SCIM. Onyx is "answering thousands of questions a week at Ramp." We treat it as the reference architecture for connector breadth and permission mirroring, and differentiate on low-latency Rust retrieval, first-class video memory, and a temporal decisions layer.

Agent memory architecture — Cloudflare Agent Memory (private beta, April 2026). The clearest published design for a production memory layer, and we adopt it nearly directly: each message gets a content-addressed SHA-256 ID for idempotent re-ingestion; an extractor runs two parallel passes (a broad ~10K-char chunking pass plus a detail pass for names, prices, and version numbers); a verifier runs eight checks; memories classify into facts, events, instructions, and tasks, with facts and instructions keyed by normalized topic, where new memories supersede rather than delete old ones.

Temporal knowledge graphs — Zep / Graphiti. Source of the bi-temporal edge model (valid time vs ingestion time) and edge-invalidation-over-deletion, which is what makes "this Slack decision supersedes that Confluence page" expressible and citable.

Memory-router proxying: a transparent LLM proxy that intercepts calls and injects user/org context, adoptable by changing only the API base URL. We implement this as our LLM gateway with memory injection — it makes Cortex usable by existing internal apps with a one-line change.
Memory API distinct from RAG: fact extraction, per-user profiles, contradiction handling, and explicit forgetting — evaluated on benchmarks like LongMemEval, LoCoMo, and ConvoMem rather than on retrieval metrics alone.
MCP-native access + browser extension: memory as a tool surface for agents and IDEs, not just a web app.
A1. Executive Summary

Cortex ingests enterprise content (chat, docs, code, tickets, CRM, meetings/video), builds hybrid + late-interaction retrieval over Qdrant, maintains a temporal memory/decisions layer, and serves grounded, cited answers via search, chat, Slack/Teams bots, browser extension, and MCP. Polyglot split: Rust on the hot retrieval/inference-gateway path; Go for connectors, orchestration, and control plane; thin Python for ML/ASR model serving.

Design Principles
Permission-parity: never return anything the user can't already see in the source. Enforce at query time (late-binding) and index ACLs into Qdrant payloads (early-binding) — defense in depth.
Retrieval quality is a pipeline, not a component: hybrid (dense+sparse) → RRF fusion → cross-encoder rerank is baseline. Naive "embed → top-k → generate" fails ~40% of the time at retrieval in production.
Freshness beats completeness: a decision in a Slack thread supersedes a stale Confluence page.
Open-source, self-hostable throughout; BYO-LLM, including fully air-gapped.
Everything is observable and evaluable: OpenTelemetry traces span ingestion→retrieval→generation; CI gates on retrieval metrics.
Non-Goals
Not a system-of-record; Cortex is read-only against sources (except optional "memory" write-back).
Not a general chatbot platform; the LLM is pluggable/BYO.
v1 targets near-real-time (seconds–minutes) freshness, not sub-second event streaming.
A2. High-Level Architecture (control / ingestion / retrieval planes)

A3. Service Inventory
Service	Lang	Responsibility	API	Scaling	Why this language

embed-gateway	Rust	Batches embed requests, routes to TEI/vLLM, backpressure	gRPC	Stateless	Batching efficiency
llm-gateway	Rust (or wrap LiteLLM)	Model routing, fallbacks, budget caps, per-tenant policy, prompt cache, memory injection	Connect/OpenAI-compat	Stateless	Single-digit-ms overhead on hot path
connector-workers	Go (Temporal SDK, river/asynq)	Per-source fetch/sync, rate-limit handling, incremental cursors	internal	Per-connector pools	Concurrency ergonomics, mature SDKs
ingestion-orchestrator	Go	Temporal workflows: backfill + incremental	gRPC	Horizontal	Durable workflow ecosystem

control-plane API	Go (connectrpc, sqlc, otel-go)	Admin, tenant, policy, SCIM, audit	Connect	Horizontal	CRUD-heavy, team velocity

web frontend	TypeScript (React 19/Vite)	UI	—	CDN/static	—

Language rationale (Go vs Rust), with data: Rust's advantage "bites at the tail." Benchmarks show a Rust (tonic) gRPC server using only 16 MB RAM as the most CPU-efficient implementation, while Go shows "a significant spike in p99 latency" under load; one production migration reported Rust p99 310 ms vs Go 1,550 ms (5×) under 25K RPS because "Go's GC is excellent, but it is a GC… Rust has no stop-the-world pauses." Discord's canonical pattern — most backend stays Go, the one hot cache-scanning path moved to Rust — is exactly our split. Go keeps its edge for the connector fleet: goroutine concurrency, mature Temporal/Kafka/gRPC SDKs, and developer velocity dominate there, where model latency dwarfs GC jitter. Python is unavoidable only for ML/ASR/parse (libraries are Python-native), isolated behind gRPC.

A4. Data Model

Postgres core entities (per-tenant schema, or shared with tenant_id partition):

source(id, tenant_id, type, config, auth_ref, status)
document(id, source_id, external_id, canonical_url, title, author_person_id, content_hash SHA-256 for idempotent re-ingest, created_at, updated_at, deleted_at tombstone, acl_ref, source_trust_weight)
chunk(id, document_id, ordinal, text, context_prefix for contextual retrieval, token_count, qdrant_point_id, embedding_model_version)
memory(id, tenant_id, type[fact|decision|event|instruction|task], normalized_topic, statement, valid_from, valid_to [bi-temporal], ingested_at, superseded_by, provenance_document_ids[], confidence)
entity/person(email, name, teams, manager_id) + expertise_edge(person_id, topic, evidence_doc_ids[], weight)
sync_run(id, source_id, started_at, cursor_before, cursor_after, items, errors, status)
citation(answer_id, chunk_id, deep_link, char_span)
permission_tuple mirror (reconciliation with SpiceDB)

Qdrant collections — single collection per embedding model + payload-based multitenancy (Qdrant's official guidance: "In most cases, a single collection per embedding model with payload-based partitioning for different tenants and use cases."). Payload index on tenant_id with is_tenant=true; plus acl_group_ids[], source_type, document_id, updated_at, is_deleted. Named vectors: dense (Qwen3-Embedding), sparse (BM25/SPLADE for native hybrid + server-side fusion), optional colbert multivector for late interaction. Use tiered multitenancy (Qdrant 1.16): small tenants share a fallback shard; "whale" tenants are promoted to dedicated shards transparently; beyond ~100k tenants use custom sharding by tenant-ID hash. Never one-collection-per-tenant — a real user "hit the 1000 collection limit after a year… and had to migrate to payload partitioning."

Object store (MinIO/S3): s3://{tenant}/raw/{source}/{doc_id} · /media/{recording_id}.mp4 · /derived/transcripts/ · /derived/keyframes/.

A5. Ingestion Pipeline (stage by stage + failure handling)
Fetch (Go connector-worker as an idempotent Temporal activity): incremental via webhook or cursor; each item → content-addressed SHA-256 for idempotent re-ingest.
Normalize → canonical Document model; capture ACLs + permalink + author.
Raw persist to object store; emit ContentEvent to NATS JetStream (at-least-once; idempotency key = content hash; DLQ + max-deliver; poison messages parked after N attempts).
Parse (Unstructured/Docling; Surya or PaddleOCR for scans/tables; ColPali path for slide decks as images).
Chunk (Rust): recursive/structural default; AST-aware (tree-sitter) for code; speaker-turn/topic-segment for transcripts; parent-child hierarchical for long docs.
Contextualize (cheap LLM, prompt-cached): prepend a 50–100-token context to each chunk. Anthropic's own numbers (Sept 2024): "Contextual Embeddings reduced the top-20-chunk retrieval failure rate by 35% (5.7% → 3.7%). Combining Contextual Embeddings and Contextual BM25 reduced failure rate by 49% (5.7% → 2.9%). Adding reranking further reduced failure rate by 67% (5.7% → 1.9%)." Cost with prompt caching ≈ ~$1.02 per million document tokens. Caveat: a widely-cited critique notes reranking + BM25 alone gets 5.7%→3.5% without contextualization on some domains — so we gate the contextualize step behind per-corpus eval.
Embed (TEI/vLLM GPU) → dense + sparse; store int8/binary-quantized in Qdrant.
Index upsert Qdrant + Postgres metadata.
Memory extraction (async): two-pass extraction (broad + detail); dedup; conflict-resolve; write to memory + graph.

Backfill smoothing (the "initial spike" problem): Temporal workflows with bounded concurrency + rate-limit-aware backoff; token-bucket per source; schedule embedding backfill off-peak; cap GPU spend via queue depth. Bound retries — a Temporal connector workflow with unbounded retries averages ~156 actions/run vs ~8 happy-path; set MaxAttempts, higher MaximumInterval, and NonRetryableErrorTypes for permission/validation errors; use a workflow timer (not a process sleep) for rate-limit backoff.

A6. Retrieval / Query Path — p99 Latency Budget

Targets (excluding LLM generation): retrieval p50 ≈ 105 ms, p95 ≈ 400 ms, p99 ≈ 800 ms.

Stage	Service	p50	p95	p99
Auth + group expansion (cached)	authz/Redis	3 ms	10 ms	25 ms
Query understanding (rewrite/HyDE, optional)	Rust/LLM	20 ms	120 ms	250 ms
ACL filter build	query-gateway	2 ms	6 ms	12 ms
Hybrid search (dense+sparse, RRF, top-100)	Qdrant	25 ms	70 ms	150 ms
Rerank top-100→top-10 (cross-encoder, GPU)	reranker	40 ms	120 ms	300 ms
Context assembly + dedup/canonicalize	query-gateway	10 ms	30 ms	60 ms
Retrieval subtotal		~105 ms	~400 ms	~800 ms
LLM TTFT (self-hosted 70B FP8)	llm-gateway	250 ms	600 ms	1.2 s
A7. Video / Audio Pipeline (first-class)
Acquire — build vs buy. Recommend buy for v1 via Recall.ai unified bot API — one endpoint joins/records/transcribes across Zoom, Meet, Teams, Webex, Slack Huddles; $0.50 per recording hour (dropped from $0.70 in early 2026, no platform fee, prorated to the second, 5 free hours), built-in transcription +$0.15/hr, storage 7 days free then $0.05/hr for 30-day retention. Recall estimates building/operating bots "takes 3–5 engineers"; a custom build ≈ 4 vCPU/concurrent bot (~$0.40/hr) plus perpetual browser-automation maintenance. Build native paths in v2 where data residency forbids third-party bots: Google Meet (Meet REST API + Drive MP4 export; requires Workspace Business Standard+; Meet-API transcript entries deleted 30 days post-conference; download via Drive REST API which does not override Drive permissions), Zoom (recording.completed webhook with download_token — no polling), Teams (Graph callRecording GA API, metered/paid; subscribe tenant-wide via communications/onlineMeetings/getAllRecordings; distinct from callRecords usage/diagnostics, retained 30 days).
ASR: WhisperX (faster-whisper/CTranslate2 backend, batched) — up to 70× real-time on an RTX 4090; word-level timestamps (±50 ms) via wav2vec2 forced alignment; pyannote diarization. int8 compute halves VRAM. Cost anchor: ~100 hours of audio ≈ $1.28 on an L40S at spot. Run diarization in a separate process to avoid the WhisperX+pyannote VRAM spike.
Chunk: speaker-turn + topic-segment; each chunk keeps a timestamp range → deep-link back to t= in the player.
Visual: keyframe extraction + slide OCR; ColPali / ColQwen2.5 late-interaction over slides-as-images (bypasses OCR; each page → ~1030 patch tokens × 128-dim; MaxSim scoring; ColQwen2 beats ColPali by ~4.7 nDCG@5 on ViDoRe).
GPU sizing: dedicated L40S/A100 ASR pool; batch jobs off-peak; RTF ~0.17 single-T4, ~0.02 dual-T4 for long-form ASR.
A8. Memory Layer (distinct from retrieval)

Combining the Zep/Graphiti temporal-graph model with the Cloudflare Agent Memory extraction pattern:

Extraction: two passes (broad ~10K-char chunk + detail pass for names/versions/numbers); classify into fact | event | instruction | task | decision.
Bi-temporal model: every memory edge tracks valid time (true in the world) + ingestion/system time; Graphiti tracks four timestamps (t_valid, t_invalid, t_created, t_expired). New facts supersede via edge invalidation, not deletion — history is preserved for citation.
Conflict/supersession: facts/instructions keyed by normalized topic; newest wins. This is exactly how a Slack-thread decision overrides a stale Confluence page: memory-service tags both to the same topic, sets the Confluence memory's valid_to = decision time, and links superseded_by.
Provenance: bidirectional index memory↔source episodes ("semantic artifacts can be traced to their sources for citation") — enables the decisions timeline and grounded answers.
Decay/forgetting: TTL on ephemeral tasks; periodic consolidation jobs.
Graph store: Postgres + Apache AGE in v1 (avoid a separate Neo4j operational burden). Honest assessment: the temporal graph earns its complexity for decisions + expertise ("who knows about X"); full GraphRAG entity-graphs are deferred — Microsoft GraphRAG is widely criticized as expensive (LLM cost on every ingest), so a LightRAG-style middle path is the fallback if the graph proves valuable.
A9. Permission Model & Enforcement (the hardest problem)
Hybrid binding: early-binding (index acl_group_ids[] into Qdrant payloads → fast pre-filter) plus late-binding (SpiceDB check on final candidates → correctness). Onyx validates this approach: "permission-aware retrieval that respects source system access controls." Red-team tests (SpiceDB + Testcontainers) must prove unauthorized chunks never reach the LLM — OWASP LLM Top-10 flags Sensitive Information Disclosure and Vector/Embedding Weaknesses.
SpiceDB (recommended): most Zanzibar-faithful; ZedToken consistency tokens ensure a check is "at least as fresh as the causality token" — critical because "if you remove a user from a sensitive group, that change must propagate instantly." Alternatives considered: OpenFGA (Auth0/Okta ecosystem, HIGHER_CONSISTENCY mode routing reads to primary) and Permify (developer-friendly, built-in data filtering). SpiceDB chosen for consistency guarantees + maturity.
Group expansion cached in Redis (pre-warm + TTL jitter to avoid stampede); SCIM/Okta/Entra ID/Google Directory sync via control plane.
ACL drift & deletions: tombstones on delete; every sync reconciles ACLs; "shared-to-everyone" edge cases flagged and gated by admin policy.
PII/DLP: Microsoft Presidio for detection/redaction at ingest; per-source redaction rules in admin.
Tenant isolation: payload partitioning default; dedicated collections/shards only where compliance mandates per-tenant encryption keys (Qdrant: "the exception, not the default").
Right-to-be-forgotten: deletion propagates Postgres tombstone → Qdrant point delete → object-store purge → memory invalidation, all audit-logged. Compliance surface: SOC 2, ISO 27001, GDPR, HIPAA, data residency, EU AI Act.
A10. API Design
Internal: gRPC/Connect-RPC + protobuf (tonic Rust server benchmarked at 16 MB RAM and best CPU-efficiency vs grpc-go).
Browser: Connect-Web + protobuf-es + TanStack Query. Buf reports connect-web bundles ~80% smaller than grpc-web, works over HTTP/1.1, and needs no Envoy proxy (gRPC-Web requires a translating proxy and lacks full streaming). 2026 guidance: "Connect-RPC if you want type-safe contracts without REST boilerplate."
Streaming tokens: SSE (simplest, proxy-friendly) for answer streaming with progressive citation reveal; WebSocket reserved for future bidirectional needs.
GraphQL: rejected — no clear win here. A typed REST/OpenAPI surface is offered for the public SDK/compatibility.
proto
service Retrieval {
  rpc Search(SearchRequest) returns (SearchResponse);
  rpc Ask(AskRequest) returns (stream AskChunk);   // SSE-bridged to the browser
}
message AskChunk {
  oneof payload { string token = 1; Citation citation = 2; Done done = 3; }
}
message Citation { string doc_id=1; string deep_link=2; string source_type=3; float score=4; }
A11. Message Queue / Streaming / Orchestration
(a) High-throughput ingestion event bus → NATS JetStream: single ~15 MB binary, sub-3 ms p50, dramatically lower ops burden than Kafka (enterprises "hate operating Kafka"). Fallback: Redpanda where Kafka-API compatibility/ecosystem is required (implements the full Kafka protocol, no ZooKeeper, ~10× lower p99 tail).
(b) Durable long-running connector workflows → Temporal: durable execution survives worker crashes; default retry = exponential backoff (2.0 coefficient, 1 s→100 s cap). Activities must be idempotent (at-least-once); use idempotency keys from stable IDs. Bound retries (see A5).
(c) Low-latency internal RPC → Connect/gRPC direct.
DLQ / idempotency / backpressure: JetStream DLQ + max-deliver; idempotency key = content SHA-256; at-least-once with dedupe (true exactly-once is avoided as impractical); backpressure via bounded consumer concurrency.
A12. Retrieval Architecture (intellectual core)
Hybrid search: dense (Qwen3-Embedding) + sparse (BM25/SPLADE) fused via Reciprocal Rank Fusion — "15–30% better retrieval accuracy than pure vector"; keyword wins for acronyms, error codes, SKUs, IDs, names (e.g., "1099-MISC"). Qdrant does native server-side fusion.
Reranking: cross-encoder (BGE-reranker-v2-m3 or Qwen3-Reranker) on top-100→top-10 — the "secret sauce" that fixes lost-in-the-middle. ColBERT late-interaction as the scale-friendly alternative.
Embedding model: Qwen3-Embedding-8B — Apache 2.0, and per Qwen's blog "ranks No.1 in the MTEB multilingual leaderboard (as of June 5, 2025, score 70.58)"; supports 100+ languages, instruction-aware, Matryoshka dims (32–1024). Cheaper tiers: 0.6B/4B. BGE-M3 as a multilingual/multi-function fallback. Serve via Text Embeddings Inference (TEI) or Infinity; binary-quantize for storage.
Query understanding: rewriting, decomposition, HyDE, multi-query, acronym/entity expansion via an org glossary, time-sensitivity routing.
Agentic vs single-shot: default single-shot + rerank (fast/cheap/good-enough); agentic multi-step only for "deep research" queries where the user tolerates ~15 s. Self-RAG/CRAG verification optional. Practitioner consensus: "agentic RAG is the right architecture for hard questions… overkill for simple 'find me a chunk' queries."
Freshness/authority: recency boost + source-trust weighting; near-duplicate collapsing across Slack/Notion/email (canonicalization by content hash + semantic dedup).
Grounding: inline citations with deep links (message permalink, Jira issue, video timestamp); abstention ("I don't know") when top rerank score is below threshold.
Storage split: Qdrant (vectors); Postgres+AGE (metadata + graph; pgvector only for tiny tenants); Qdrant sparse or Tantivy (Rust BM25) for keyword; ClickHouse for analytics/eval logs; MinIO for raw/media.
A13. Qdrant Specifics
HNSW tuning: m 16–32, ef_construct 128–256, query-time ef traded for recall/latency.
Quantization math: float32 768-dim ≈ 3 GB per 1 M vectors; 1024-dim ≈ 5.72 GB/M (×1.5 for metadata/indexes). Binary quantization gives up to 32× compression — Qdrant's own math: a 1536-dim vector 6 KB→192 bytes, i.e. ~6.14 GB/M → ~192 MB/M (a derived estimate puts 10 M 1536-dim vectors at ~1.92 GB RAM under BQ vs ~61.4 GB float32). Best practice: originals on_disk=true, quantized always_ram=true, rescore top candidates; enable BQ above ~100K vectors; BQ works best on ≥1024-dim, zero-centered models.
Payload indexes on tenant_id/acl/source_type/updated_at; ACORN (1.16) improves filtered search.
Ops: distributed sharding/replication; snapshots for backup; collection aliases for zero-downtime reindex/tenant rebuilds.
Monitoring: Prometheus /metrics per peer + Grafana dashboards.
A14. LLM Serving in a Self-Hosted Enterprise
Engine: vLLM default (PagedAttention + continuous batching; largest ecosystem; HF Inference Endpoints default to it). TGI is EOL — HF put it into maintenance mode on Dec 11, 2025, recommending vLLM/SGLang; repo archived read-only March 2026. SGLang for prefix-heavy agent/RAG workloads (RadixAttention): ~29% higher throughput than vLLM at 8B (≈16,200 vs 12,500 tok/s on H100), narrowing to 3–5% at 70B.
Models: Llama-3.3-70B / Qwen / DeepSeek / Mistral / gpt-oss / Gemma. Llama-3.3-70B FP8 ≈ 70 GB weights → tight on 1×H100 80 GB; 32k context + 10 concurrent users ≈ 3×H100 (FP8 KV: 56 GB cache + 140 GB weights ≈ 196 GB). A single H200 FP8 70B >3,800 tok/s/GPU; 8×H100 MLPerf ≈ 24,525 tok/s aggregate.
BYO-API vs air-gapped: Bedrock / Vertex AI / Azure OpenAI / Anthropic via the gateway; fully air-gapped mode = local vLLM only.
Gateway (LiteLLM-style): 140+ providers, ordered fallback chains (+ context-window/content-policy fallbacks), hard budget caps per key/team/org (429 at cap, Redis cross-pod counter), per-tenant model policy, prompt caching, structured outputs. Route to self-hosted GPUs first, fall back to cloud APIs at capacity ("cut inference costs 60–80%"); ~single-digit-ms overhead.
Capacity planning: 1k seats ≈ 1–2×H100 (or BYO-API); 10k ≈ 4–8×H100 + autoscale; 50k ≈ dedicated GPU fleet + SGLang + aggressive prompt caching.
A15. Observability & Evaluation
Stack: OpenTelemetry end-to-end (traces span ingestion→retrieval→generation); Grafana LGTM (Loki/Grafana/Tempo/Mimir) or SigNoz; ClickHouse for high-cardinality eval logs; Prometheus/VictoriaMetrics.
LLM-specific: Langfuse (self-hostable, open source) + OpenLLMetry/Traceloop; OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions.
SLIs/SLOs: retrieval p95 < 700 ms; answer TTFT p95 < 1.5 s; sync freshness p95 < 5 min; citation accuracy > 90%.
RAG eval strategy: golden Q&A set (minimum 100 questions before iterating), Ragas/DeepEval/promptfoo; recall@k, nDCG, MRR, faithfulness/groundedness, answer relevance, citation accuracy (measure retrieval and faithfulness independently — "an LLM that faithfully echoes retrieved content still gives wrong answers if retrieval returned the wrong chunks"). Online signals: thumbs, copy events, "answer accepted," click-through. CI regression gate on the eval set; drift detection. Beware LLM-as-judge bias.
Cold-start eval: synthesize a golden set from ingested docs (LLM-generated Q&A reviewed by SMEs) before any user traffic.
A16. Deployment (GCP / AWS / Azure)
Kubernetes + Helm (+ Kustomize overlays); Operator for stateful pieces; Terraform modules per cloud (EKS/GKE/AKS, RDS/Cloud SQL/Azure DB, S3/GCS/Blob, GPU node pools + instance types). Cloud-managed dependency substitution supported.
docker-compose "evaluation mode" single-node (mirrors Onyx's one-command install).
Air-gapped: image mirroring, offline model bundles, telemetry-off license mode.
Sizing tiers: Eval (1 node) / 1k-seat / 10k-seat / 50k-seat.
HA/DR: multi-AZ; Qdrant replication; Postgres HA; snapshot backup/restore.
Zero-downtime reindex / re-embedding 100M chunks: dual-write to a new collection under a new embedding_model_version, backfill via queue, run eval, then alias cutover.
Licensing: open-core — Apache 2.0 core + BSL/commercial Enterprise for SSO/SCIM/RBAC/advanced connectors/audit. Precedents: Onyx = MIT core + Enterprise license for ee/; Grafana relicensed to AGPLv3 (2021); Qdrant Apache 2.0; BSL (used by CockroachDB/HashiCorp) gives a commercial-exclusivity window then converts to Apache. Avoid AGPL for the SDK to ease adoption; consider it for the server core to deter SaaS cloning.
A17. Scalability Limits & Failure Modes (what breaks first, at what scale)
Slack ingestion — the #1 risk. Per Slack's official changelog, conversations.history/conversations.replies for non-Marketplace commercially-distributed apps drop from Tier 3 to 1 request/minute with a maximum of 15 objects/request (existing installs subject as of March 3, 2026). Internal customer-built apps retain the old limits (1,000 messages/request at 50+ req/min); Marketplace apps are exempt. Mitigations: ship as an internal customer-built app, get Marketplace-approved, or use the Enterprise Grid Discovery API (org-wide, read-only, JSON, compliance-scoped — sees every message/file/DM including edits/deletes). The Events API (30,000 event deliveries/hr/workspace) is preferred for real-time.
Embedding backfill GPU spend spikes on initial sync → smooth via bounded queues (A5).
Qdrant RAM blows up if BQ isn't enabled at scale.
ACL group-expansion cache stampede on large directories → pre-warm + TTL jitter.
Temporal action explosion from unbounded retries.

Other connector mechanics baked into the design: Jira/Confluence Cloud now share a points-based rate model (base 1 point/request + per-object; Tier-1 global pool shared across tenants) — prefer webhooks + incremental updated >= "-5m" JQL / CQL lastmodified >= now("-5m") (mind the CQL 50-result cap when expanding body). Google Drive changes.list + page tokens; watch channels expire at max 7 days (changes) → automated renewal required; changes.list can't filter by folder (client-side filter); Docs via files.export; domain-wide delegation for headless service accounts. Microsoft Graph delta queries + change notifications (driveItem/users/groups/messages delta; delta tokens can 410 resyncRequired). GitHub: split load across REST (5,000 req/hr) and GraphQL (5,000 points/hr) budgets; heed secondary limits (100 concurrent, 900 pts/min REST, 2,000 pts/min GraphQL).

A18. Testing Strategy (incl. retrieval quality in CI)

Unit + proto-driven contract tests; connector integration tests against sandbox tenants; retrieval quality in CI via the golden set with hard nDCG/recall gates (fail the build on regression); load tests (k6/wrk) for p99; chaos tests on worker crashes (Temporal replay); permission red-team tests (SpiceDB + Testcontainers) asserting unauthorized chunks never surface.

A19. Phased Roadmap (with team sizing)
v0 (0–3 mo, 4–6 eng): core ingestion (Slack, GDrive, Confluence, GitHub), Qdrant hybrid search + rerank, basic web UI, SpiceDB permissions, docker-compose eval mode.
v1 (3–6 mo, 8–10 eng): Jira/Teams/Notion, memory layer, Slack bot, citations/deep links, Langfuse eval harness, Helm/Terraform, admin console.
v2 (6–12 mo): video/audio (Recall.ai + native), ColPali visual retrieval, expert finder/people graph, browser extension, MCP, connector SDK.
v3 (12 mo+): agentic deep research, temporal decisions timeline, 50k-seat scale, air-gapped GA, marketplace connectors.

Connector roadmap (phased): v1 = Slack, Google Workspace, Confluence, Jira, GitHub, Notion, Teams (highest-value, best-documented APIs). v2 = GitLab/Bitbucket, Linear, Salesforce, Zendesk, SharePoint/OneDrive, Gmail/Outlook, meetings (Zoom/Meet/Teams/Gong/Fireflies). v3 = Asana/ClickUp/Monday, Figma/Miro/Airtable, Snowflake/BigQuery/dbt/Looker metadata, PagerDuty/Opsgenie/Datadog, Workday/BambooHR/Greenhouse (people graph), generic (S3/GCS/Blob, SFTP, RSS, web crawler via Firecrawl, custom REST/webhook, email-in, CLI/SDK push). Connector SDK: a language-neutral interface (Fetch, Normalize→Document, GetACLs, Cursor, Webhook) so customers/community write their own — the differentiator vs closed platforms.

A20. Key Technology Decisions Table
Concern	Chosen	Alternatives (rejected)	One-line rationale
Hot-path language	Rust	Go, C++	No GC → flat p99 under streaming (16 MB tonic; 5× better tail in migrations)
Connector language	Go	Rust, Python	Goroutine concurrency + mature SDKs
ML/ASR/parse language	Python	—	Libraries are Python-native
Vector DB	Qdrant	Milvus, Weaviate, pgvector	Open, quantization, native hybrid + fusion, tiered multitenancy
Authz	SpiceDB	OpenFGA, Permify, Cerbos	Most Zanzibar-faithful; ZedToken consistency
Event bus	NATS JetStream	Kafka, Redpanda, Pulsar	Lowest ops burden, sub-3 ms; Redpanda fallback
Durable workflows	Temporal	Cadence, Restate, River/Asynq	Durable execution, retries, replay
Internal API	Connect/gRPC	REST, GraphQL	Typed, fast, streaming
Browser API	Connect-Web + protobuf-es	gRPC-Web, tRPC	80% smaller bundle, no proxy
Embeddings	Qwen3-Embedding-8B	BGE-M3, Nomic v2, Jina v3/4	#1 MTEB multilingual 70.58, Apache 2.0
Reranker	BGE-reranker-v2-m3	Qwen3-Reranker, mxbai, Cohere	Open, strong, self-hostable
LLM engine	vLLM (+SGLang)	TGI (EOL), llama.cpp, Ollama	TGI maintenance-mode Dec 2025; vLLM ecosystem
ASR	WhisperX + pyannote	NeMo, Canary, Parakeet	70× RT, word timestamps, diarization
Visual retrieval	ColPali/ColQwen	OCR pipelines	Slides-as-images, no brittle OCR
Graph	Postgres + Apache AGE	Neo4j, FalkorDB	Avoid extra DB ops burden in v1
Observability	OTel + Grafana LGTM + Langfuse	SigNoz, Arize/Phoenix	Open, self-hostable, GenAI conventions

A21. Key Risks & Explicit Tradeoffs
Slack rate limits (see A17) — architectural mitigation required, not optional.
Permission-parity — the difference between a product and a breach; hybrid binding + red-team CI.
GPU cost is the dominant TCO — BYO-API is the escape hatch.
Graph complexity — ship after core retrieval proves value; don't over-invest in GraphRAG.
Contextual retrieval isn't universal — gate behind per-corpus eval; some domains gain little.

lines.text: # Cortex — the company's brain
Cortex ingests enterprise content (chat, docs, code, tickets, CRM, meetings and video),
builds hybrid and late-interaction retrieval over Qdrant, maintains a temporal
memory/decisions layer, and serves grounded, cited answers through search, chat,
Slack/Teams bots, a browser extension, and MCP.
It is open-source and self-hostable end to end, with a bring-your-own LLM
(including fully air-gapped operation).
## Design principles
- **Permission parity.** Never return anything the user could not already open in the
source system. Enforced twice — ACLs indexed into the vector payload (early binding)
*and* rechecked per candidate at query time (late binding).
- **Retrieval quality is a pipeline, not a component.** Hybrid dense + sparse search,
RRF fusion, then cross-encoder reranking is the baseline. Naive "embed → top-k →
generate" fails at the retrieval step roughly 40% of the time in production.
- **Freshness beats completeness.** A decision in a Slack thread supersedes a stale
Confluence page, and the system models that explicitly.
- **Everything is observable and evaluable.** OpenTelemetry traces span
ingestion → retrieval → generation; CI gates on retrieval metrics.
### Non-goals
- Not a system of record — Cortex is read-only against sources, apart from optional
memory write-back.
- Not a general chatbot platform — the LLM is pluggable.
- v1 targets near-real-time freshness (seconds to minutes), not sub-second event streaming.
## System architecture
The system splits into three planes: a Go **control plane** for tenants, connectors,
policy and audit; an **ingestion plane** of Go workers plus Rust CPU services and thin
Python ML services; and a Rust **retrieval plane** on the hot path.
<!-- lucid-diagram:cortex-system-architecture -->
![Cortex — System Architecture](docs/cortex-system-architecture.svg)
Cortex is a self-hostable company brain: it ingests enterprise content, builds hybrid retrieval over it, maintains a temporal memory layer, and serves grounded, cited answers.

The system splits into three planes. The **control plane** (Go) owns tenants, connector configuration, SCIM/SSO sync, policy, and audit. The **ingestion plane** pulls from SaaS sources through Temporal-orchestrated Go workers, persists raw payloads to object storage, and emits content-addressed events onto NATS JetStream for the parse → chunk → contextualize → embed pipeline. The **retrieval plane** is a Rust hot path: the Query Gateway expands permissions, runs hybrid search against Qdrant, reranks with a cross-encoder, assembles context, and streams tokens back over SSE with inline citations.

The polyglot split is deliberate. Rust carries the latency-critical path because it has no GC pauses under streaming fan-out; Go carries the connector fleet where SDK maturity and goroutine concurrency matter more than tail latency; Python is isolated behind gRPC for ML, ASR, and document parsing where the libraries are Python-native.
<!-- /lucid-diagram:cortex-system-architecture -->
### Why this language split
Rust's advantage bites at the tail. Benchmarked gRPC servers show a Rust/tonic server
holding ~16 MB RSS as the most CPU-efficient implementation, while Go shows a marked p99
spike under load; one production migration reported p99 of 310 ms on Rust against
1,550 ms on Go at 25K RPS, because a GC — however good — still pauses. Go keeps its
edge for the connector fleet, where remote API latency dwarfs GC jitter and SDK maturity
and developer velocity dominate. Python is unavoidable for ML, ASR and document parsing,
and is isolated behind gRPC so it never sits on the latency-critical path.
### Service inventory
| Service | Language | Responsibility |
| `query-gateway` | Rust (axum/tonic/tower) | Hot path: ACL → search → rerank → context → LLM, SSE streaming |
| `reranker` | Rust (ort/ONNX) | Cross-encoder / ColBERT reranking |
| `chunker` | Rust (tokenizers, rayon) | Structural, semantic and AST-aware chunking |
| `embed-gateway` | Rust | Batches embed requests, routes to TEI/vLLM, applies backpressure |
| `llm-gateway` | Rust | Model routing, fallbacks, budget caps, prompt cache, memory injection |
| `connector-workers` | Go (Temporal SDK) | Per-source fetch/sync, rate limits, incremental cursors |
| `ingestion-orchestrator` | Go | Temporal workflows for backfill and incremental sync |
| `parse-service` | Python (Docling/Unstructured) | PDF, table and OCR extraction |
| `asr-service` | Python (WhisperX + pyannote) | Transcription and diarization |
| `memory-service` | Go + LLM | Fact/decision extraction, dedup, conflict resolution, decay |
| `control-plane` | Go (connectrpc, sqlc) | Admin, tenant, policy, SCIM, audit |
| `authz` | SpiceDB | Zanzibar-style permission checks |
| `web` | TypeScript (React 19/Vite) | UI |
## Ingestion plane
<!-- lucid-diagram:cortex-ingestion-plane -->
![Cortex — Ingestion Plane](docs/cortex-ingestion-plane.svg)
The ingestion plane turns heterogeneous SaaS content into indexed, permission-tagged chunks.

Connector workers run as Temporal activities with bounded retries, honouring each source's rate-limit model. Every fetched item is normalized to a canonical Document with its ACLs and permalink, persisted raw to object storage, and announced as a ContentEvent keyed by SHA-256 so re-ingestion is idempotent. The pipeline then parses, chunks, prepends a short LLM-generated context to each chunk, embeds, and upserts to Qdrant with the metadata mirrored in Postgres. Memory extraction runs asynchronously off the same event stream.
<!-- /lucid-diagram:cortex-ingestion-plane -->
**Stages.** Fetch (idempotent Temporal activity, incremental via webhook or cursor) →
normalize to a canonical Document capturing ACLs, permalink and author → persist raw to
object storage → emit `ContentEvent` on NATS JetStream → parse → chunk → contextualize →
embed → upsert → asynchronous memory extraction.
**Contextual retrieval.** Each chunk is prefixed with a 50–100 token LLM-generated
context before embedding. Published results put the top-20 retrieval failure rate at
5.7% → 3.7% with contextual embeddings, → 2.9% adding contextual BM25, and → 1.9% adding
reranking, at roughly $1.02 per million document tokens with prompt caching. A credible
critique shows reranking plus BM25 alone reaching 3.5% on some corpora without the
contextualization step, so this stage is **gated behind per-corpus evaluation** rather
than assumed to pay for itself.
**Backfill smoothing.** The initial sync is the spike that breaks things. Bounded
workflow concurrency, a per-source token bucket, and off-peak scheduling cap GPU spend.
Retries are explicitly bounded — an unbounded-retry connector workflow averages ~156
Temporal actions per run against ~8 on the happy path — using `MaxAttempts`, a raised
`MaximumInterval`, `NonRetryableErrorTypes` for permission and validation failures, and
workflow timers rather than process sleeps for rate-limit backoff.
## Retrieval and query path
<!-- lucid-diagram:cortex-retrieval-query-path -->
![Cortex — Retrieval Query Path](docs/cortex-retrieval-query-path.svg)
The retrieval path is budgeted to roughly 105 ms p50 and 800 ms p99 before generation begins.

A query resolves permissions from cache, optionally rewrites, builds an ACL prefilter, runs dense and sparse search in parallel with server-side RRF fusion, reranks the top 100 down to 10 with a cross-encoder, rechecks authorization on the survivors, assembles context, and streams the answer with citations.
<!-- /lucid-diagram:cortex-retrieval-query-path -->
### Latency budget (excluding generation)
| Stage | Service | p50 | p95 | p99 |
| Auth + group expansion (cached) | authz / Redis | 3 ms | 10 ms | 25 ms |
| Query understanding (optional) | Rust / LLM | 20 ms | 120 ms | 250 ms |
| ACL filter build | query-gateway | 2 ms | 6 ms | 12 ms |
| Hybrid search, top-100 | Qdrant | 25 ms | 70 ms | 150 ms |
| Rerank 100 → 10 | reranker | 40 ms | 120 ms | 300 ms |
| Context assembly + dedup | query-gateway | 10 ms | 30 ms | 60 ms |
| **Retrieval subtotal** | | **~105 ms** | **~400 ms** | **~800 ms** |
| LLM TTFT (self-hosted 70B FP8) | llm-gateway | 250 ms | 600 ms | 1.2 s |
Note that the late-binding permission recheck runs *after* reranking, so it validates
roughly ten candidates rather than a hundred — correctness without paying for it in the
budget above.
**Hybrid search** fuses dense (Qwen3-Embedding) and sparse (BM25/SPLADE) results with
Reciprocal Rank Fusion, worth 15–30% retrieval accuracy over pure vector search; keyword
matching is what rescues acronyms, error codes, SKUs, IDs and names such as `1099-MISC`.
Qdrant performs the fusion server-side.
**Reranking** with a cross-encoder over the top 100 is the step that fixes
lost-in-the-middle behaviour. ColBERT-style late interaction is the scale-friendly
alternative.
**Agentic vs single-shot.** Single-shot plus rerank is the default because it is fast,
cheap and good enough. Multi-step agentic retrieval is reserved for explicit deep-research
queries where the user tolerates ~15 seconds.
**Grounding.** Answers carry inline citations with deep links — message permalink, Jira
issue, video timestamp — and the system abstains when the top rerank score falls below
threshold.
## Memory layer
<!-- lucid-diagram:cortex-memory-temporal-graph -->
![Cortex — Memory & Temporal Graph](docs/cortex-memory-temporal-graph.svg)
The memory layer is what separates Cortex from ordinary RAG: it knows what is currently true, not merely what was written.

Two extraction passes run over each episode, a verifier screens the candidates, and results classify into facts, events, instructions, tasks, and decisions. Facts and instructions are keyed by normalized topic; when a newer memory arrives on the same topic the older edge is invalidated rather than deleted, so history stays citable.
<!-- /lucid-diagram:cortex-memory-temporal-graph -->
**Bi-temporal model.** Every memory edge tracks both valid time (when the fact was true
in the world) and ingestion time (when the system learned it). New facts supersede old
ones through edge invalidation, never deletion, so the history remains available for
citation and for a decisions timeline.
**Worked example — the Slack decision that overrides Confluence.** Both artifacts are
tagged to the same normalized topic. On ingesting the newer Slack thread, the
memory service sets `valid_to` on the Confluence-derived memory to the decision
timestamp and links `superseded_by`. A later query retrieves the current fact, and can
still show what it replaced and when.
**Provenance.** A bidirectional index maps every memory back to the source episodes it
was derived from, which is what makes memory-backed answers citable rather than merely
plausible.
**Scope discipline.** The temporal graph earns its complexity for decisions and
expertise ("who knows about X"). Full GraphRAG-style entity graphs are deliberately
deferred — the LLM cost on every ingest is hard to justify — with a lighter-weight
middle path as the fallback if the graph proves its value. Postgres with Apache AGE
avoids operating a second database in v1.
## Video and audio pipeline
<!-- lucid-diagram:cortex-video-amp-audio-pipeline -->
![Cortex — Video & Audio Pipeline](docs/cortex-video-amp-audio-pipeline.svg)
Meetings are first-class memory, not an afterthought.

v1 buys capture through a unified bot API rather than operating meeting bots in-house; v2 adds native per-platform paths where data residency forbids a third party. Recordings are demuxed, transcribed with word-level alignment, diarized in a separate process to avoid a VRAM spike, chunked by speaker turn, and indexed with timestamp ranges so every citation deep-links back into the player.
<!-- /lucid-diagram:cortex-video-amp-audio-pipeline -->
**Buy before build.** A unified bot API covers Zoom, Meet, Teams, Webex and Slack
Huddles from one endpoint at roughly $0.50 per recording hour, against a self-built
fleet that costs on the order of 3–5 engineers to build and operate plus perpetual
browser-automation maintenance. Native per-platform capture lands in v2 for tenants whose
data residency rules forbid a third-party bot: Zoom via the `recording.completed` webhook
with a download token, Meet via the Meet REST API with Drive export, Teams via the Graph
`callRecording` API subscribed tenant-wide.
**ASR.** WhisperX on a faster-whisper/CTranslate2 backend reaches up to ~70× real time on
a single high-end GPU, with word-level timestamps accurate to about ±50 ms via wav2vec2
forced alignment. Diarization runs in a **separate process** — co-locating it with
WhisperX produces a VRAM spike. int8 compute halves VRAM; roughly 100 hours of audio
costs about $1.28 on spot L40S capacity.
**Visual retrieval.** Keyframes and slides are indexed as images through ColQwen-style
late interaction, which sidesteps brittle OCR entirely; each page becomes ~1030 patch
tokens scored by MaxSim.
## Permissions and control plane
<!-- lucid-diagram:cortex-permissions-amp-control-plane -->
![Cortex — Permissions & Control Plane](docs/cortex-permissions-amp-control-plane.svg)
Permission parity is the difference between a product and a breach: Cortex must never return anything a user could not already open in the source system.

Enforcement is defense in depth. Group memberships are indexed into Qdrant payloads for a fast prefilter (early binding), and the surviving candidates are rechecked against SpiceDB with a consistency token before they reach the model (late binding). SCIM sync invalidates the group cache on membership change, an ACL reconciler repairs drift on every sync, and a red-team CI suite asserts that unauthorized chunks never surface.
<!-- /lucid-diagram:cortex-permissions-amp-control-plane -->
- **SpiceDB** is chosen over OpenFGA and Permify for its consistency guarantees: ZedToken
consistency tokens make a check at least as fresh as a given causality point. This
matters concretely — removing a user from a sensitive group must take effect
immediately, which is why SCIM sync invalidates the Redis group cache directly rather
than waiting for a TTL.
- **Group expansion** is cached in Redis with pre-warming and TTL jitter to avoid a
stampede against large directories.
- **ACL drift.** Deletes leave tombstones, and every sync reconciles ACLs.
Shared-to-everyone edge cases are flagged and gated by admin policy.
- **PII/DLP.** Presidio detection and redaction at ingest, with per-source rules
configured in the admin console.
- **Right to be forgotten.** Deletion propagates from a Postgres tombstone through Qdrant
point deletion, object-store purge and memory invalidation — every step audit-logged.
- **Tenant isolation.** Payload partitioning is the default; dedicated collections or
shards are the exception, reserved for compliance regimes requiring per-tenant
encryption keys.
## Storage
**Postgres** holds sources, documents (with a SHA-256 content hash for idempotent
re-ingest and tombstones for deletes), chunks, memories, entities and expertise edges,
sync runs, citations, and a mirror of the permission tuples.
**Qdrant** uses a single collection per embedding model with payload-based multitenancy —
never one collection per tenant, a pattern that has repeatedly hit the 1000-collection
limit within a year and forced migration. A payload index on `tenant_id` with
`is_tenant=true`, plus indexes on `acl_group_ids[]`, `source_type`, `document_id`,
`updated_at` and `is_deleted`. Named vectors carry dense, sparse and optional ColBERT
multivectors. Tiered multitenancy lets small tenants share a fallback shard while whale
tenants are transparently promoted to dedicated shards.
**Quantization.** float32 at 1024 dimensions costs roughly 5.72 GB per million vectors
before metadata; binary quantization delivers up to 32× compression, taking a 1536-dim
vector from 6 KB to 192 bytes. Keep originals `on_disk=true`, quantized `always_ram=true`,
and rescore the top candidates. Enable BQ above roughly 100K vectors; it works best on
zero-centered models of 1024 dimensions or more.
**Object store** holds raw payloads, media, transcripts and keyframes.
## Key technology decisions
| Concern | Chosen | Rationale |
| Hot-path language | Rust | No GC, flat p99 under streaming |
| Connector language | Go | Goroutine concurrency, mature SDKs |
| ML / ASR / parse | Python | Libraries are Python-native |
| Vector DB | Qdrant | Quantization, native hybrid + fusion, tiered multitenancy |
| Authz | SpiceDB | Most Zanzibar-faithful; ZedToken consistency |
| Event bus | NATS JetStream | Sub-3 ms, far lower ops burden than Kafka (Redpanda as fallback) |
| Durable workflows | Temporal | Durable execution, retries, replay |
| Internal API | Connect/gRPC | Typed, fast, streaming |
| Browser API | Connect-Web + protobuf-es | ~80% smaller bundle than gRPC-Web, no proxy needed |
| Embeddings | Qwen3-Embedding-8B | Apache 2.0, top MTEB multilingual, Matryoshka dims |
| Reranker | BGE-reranker-v2-m3 | Open, strong, self-hostable |
| LLM engine | vLLM (+ SGLang) | TGI entered maintenance mode Dec 2025; vLLM has the ecosystem |
| ASR | WhisperX + pyannote | ~70× real time, word timestamps, diarization |
| Visual retrieval | ColPali / ColQwen | Slides as images, no brittle OCR |
| Graph | Postgres + Apache AGE | Avoids a second database in v1 |
| Meeting capture (v1) | Unified bot API | $0.50/hr beats a 3–5 engineer build |
| License | Apache core + BSL enterprise | Adoption plus commercial protection |
## Observability and evaluation
OpenTelemetry traces span ingestion through retrieval to generation, with Grafana LGTM
or SigNoz for the general stack, Langfuse for LLM-specific tracing, and ClickHouse for
high-cardinality evaluation logs.
**SLOs.** Retrieval p95 under 700 ms; answer TTFT p95 under 1.5 s; sync freshness p95
under 5 minutes; citation accuracy above 90%.
**Evaluation.** A golden set of at least 100 questions before any iteration, scored on
recall@k, nDCG, MRR, faithfulness and citation accuracy. Retrieval and faithfulness are
measured **independently** — a model that faithfully echoes retrieved content still
answers wrongly when retrieval returned the wrong chunks. CI fails the build on
regression against the golden set. Before user traffic exists, the golden set is
synthesized from ingested documents and reviewed by subject-matter experts. LLM-as-judge
scoring is used with known bias caveats.
## Scalability limits and failure modes
Ordered by what breaks first:
1. **Slack ingestion — the top risk.** `conversations.history` and `.replies` drop to
1 request/minute with at most 15 objects per request for non-Marketplace commercially
distributed apps. Mitigations: ship as an internal customer-built app (which retains
the old limits), get Marketplace approval, or use the Enterprise Grid Discovery API.
The Events API is preferred for real-time.
2. **Embedding backfill GPU spend** spikes on initial sync — smoothed by bounded queues.
3. **Qdrant RAM** blows up if binary quantization is not enabled at scale.
4. **ACL group-expansion cache stampede** against large directories — pre-warm and jitter.
5. **Temporal action explosion** from unbounded retries.
Other connector mechanics are baked into the design: Jira/Confluence points-based rate
limits favour webhooks plus incremental JQL/CQL; Google Drive watch channels expire after
at most 7 days and need automated renewal, and `changes.list` cannot filter by folder;
Microsoft Graph delta tokens can return 410 `resyncRequired`; GitHub load must be split
across separate REST and GraphQL budgets with secondary limits respected.
## Deployment
Kubernetes with Helm and Kustomize overlays, Terraform modules per cloud, and an
operator for the stateful components. A single-node docker-compose evaluation mode gives
a one-command install. Air-gapped operation is supported through image mirroring, offline
model bundles and a telemetry-off license mode. Sizing tiers cover evaluation, 1k, 10k
and 50k seats.
**Zero-downtime re-embedding** of ~100M chunks: dual-write into a new collection under a
new `embedding_model_version`, backfill through the queue, run the eval set, then cut
over by alias.
## Roadmap
| Phase | Scope |
| **v0** (0–3 mo, 4–6 eng) | Core ingestion (Slack, GDrive, Confluence, GitHub), Qdrant hybrid search + rerank, basic web UI, SpiceDB permissions, docker-compose eval mode |
| **v1** (3–6 mo, 8–10 eng) | Jira/Teams/Notion, memory layer, Slack bot, citations and deep links, eval harness, Helm/Terraform, admin console |
| **v2** (6–12 mo) | Video and audio, ColPali visual retrieval, expert finder, browser extension, MCP, connector SDK |
| **v3** (12 mo+) | Agentic deep research, decisions timeline, 50k-seat scale, air-gapped GA, marketplace connectors |
The **connector SDK** — a language-neutral interface of Fetch, Normalize, GetACLs, Cursor
and Webhook — is the differentiator against closed platforms, letting customers and the
community write their own sources.
